title: The Port Is Built. Now Build the Town Around It.
summary: A transhipment port creates few jobs by itself. Whether Thiruvananthapuram benefits depends on the logistics, housing, skills and services that grow around it, and on planning that starts now.
body: scholar-two Vizhinjam Ports Urban planning maritime-economy urbanisation The Vizhinjam International Seaport has been discussed for so long that its arrival can feel like the end of a story. It is the beginning of one. Transhipment ports move containers from very large ships to smaller ones. Much of that cargo never leaves the port. A port of this kind can be highly automated, which means that the number of jobs inside the gate is modest. The larger economic effect comes from what develops around it: logistics parks, ship services, warehousing, repair, finance, hospitality, and the housing and services that the people working in them need. None of that happens automatically. Ports elsewhere in the world have become engines of regional growth where land, transport links and skills were planned in advance. They have become enclaves, surrounded by congestion and resentment, where they were not. Three things should be at the top of the agenda. First, a plan for the land around the port. Without one, speculation and unplanned building will make good development harder and more expensive. The plan should protect fishing villages and their access to the sea. Second, connections that work. Road and rail links to the port must be designed to keep heavy freight out of residential streets and away from the city's already crowded roads. Third, skills for local people. Training programs for port, logistics and maritime jobs should be designed with employers now, with places reserved for young people from the coastal communities most affected by the port. The port is a large public investment. Its return will be measured not in containers handled, but in what it does for the people of Thiruvananthapuram and the coast. [Placeholder publication. title: Bringing Off Budget Borrowing into the Light
summary: Borrowing by state owned bodies has become a large and contested part of public finance. A simple annual disclosure statement would let legislators and citizens see the full picture without stopping investment.
body: scholar-one State finances Public debt Transparency governance-finance-accountability federalism The problem Indian states increasingly finance roads, bridges, hospitals and other public assets through borrowing by special purpose bodies and public sector undertakings, rather than directly through the state budget. This has allowed investment that the state could not otherwise afford within its borrowing limits. It has also made it harder for legislators, auditors and citizens to see the total obligations that the state has taken on, and how they will be repaid. The question has become politically charged, with disputes between the Union and states over whether such borrowing should count against state borrowing limits. Lost in the dispute is a simpler point on which all sides should agree: whatever the accounting rule, the public deserves to know the numbers. What we found Our review of state budget documents found that: - information on borrowing by state bodies is spread across several documents, in different formats and at different dates - repayment obligations that will fall on the state budget in future years are rarely set out in one place - guarantees given by the state to lenders are disclosed, but their likely cost is not estimated - legislators receive little time or analytical support to examine these figures Recommendations 1. Publish an annual Statement of Extended Public Liabilities alongside the budget, listing borrowing by every state owned body that is serviced wholly or partly from the budget, with the repayment schedule for the next ten years. 2. Estimate the expected cost of guarantees , not only their face value, using a published method. 3. Refer the statement to the Committee on Estimates or a new fiscal committee of the legislature for examination each year. 4. Ask the state's auditor to certify the statement within six months of the end of the financial year. Why this matters Transparency does not settle the argument about how much a state should borrow. It makes that argument possible on the basis of shared facts. A state that discloses its full obligations will find it easier to defend its borrowing to lenders, to the Union and to its own citizens. title: Five Books for Anyone Starting Out in Indian Public Policy
summary: Fellows and interns often ask where to begin. Here is a short reading list, chosen for clarity, range and the arguments they will provoke.
body: mentor-one Reading list Learning institutions-and-social-justice state-and-politics Every new cohort of fellows and interns asks the same question in their first week: what should I read? There is no single answer, but here are five books that have repaid the time of many people starting out. They disagree with each other in useful ways. 1. Jean Drèze and Amartya Sen, An Uncertain Glory: India and Its Contradictions (2013). A sustained argument that India's growth has not been matched by progress in health, education and public services, with frequent reference to Kerala's experience. 2. Devesh Kapur, Pratap Bhanu Mehta and Milan Vaishnav (eds.), Rethinking Public Institutions in India (2017). Essays on the institutions that actually run the country, from the Election Commission to the civil services. Essential for understanding why good policies often fail in implementation. 3. Robin Jeffrey, Politics, Women and Well-Being: How Kerala Became 'a Model' (1992). A historian's account of how social movements, politics and the position of women shaped Kerala's distinctive development. 4. Abhijit V. Banerjee and Esther Duflo, Poor Economics (2011). A readable introduction to evidence based thinking about poverty, and to the careful testing of policy ideas. 5. Y. V. Reddy and G. R. Reddy, Indian Fiscal Federalism (2019). A clear guide to how money flows between the Union and the states, by authors with long experience of the system. Read them with a pencil. Note where you disagree, and why. The habit of arguing with what you read is the most useful thing a reading list can teach. [Placeholder publication. Replace or update the list as you wish.]

title: What Three Decades of Decentralisation Have Taught Us
summary: A practitioner reflects on what Kerala's experiment in local democracy achieved, what it did not, and what the next generation of reform should look like.
body: adviser-one Decentralisation Local government federalism governance-finance-accountability When Kerala decided in the mid 1990s to hand a large share of its development budget to panchayats and municipalities, many experienced administrators expected chaos. Funds would be wasted, they said; local leaders lacked the capacity; the departments would never let go. Some of those fears proved justified. Many did not. Looking back across three decades, a few lessons stand out. Money and power must travel together. Where local governments received both funds and real authority over institutions, they used them, sometimes imperfectly, but often creatively. Where they received funds with tight central conditions, they became implementing agencies rather than governments. Participation needs care. The early years of the People's Plan Campaign mobilised extraordinary public participation. Sustaining it has proved much harder. Grama sabhas in many places have become formalities. Participation has to be renewed, not assumed. Capacity follows responsibility. Local governments that were given real responsibility developed capacity faster than those that were not. Training helps, but nothing builds capacity like having to deliver. Departments must change too. Decentralisation is not only about local government. It requires state departments to shift from running things to supporting and regulating those who do. The next generation of reform should focus on own revenue, on professional support for smaller local governments, and on restoring the democratic energy that made the experiment remarkable in the first place. The views expressed are the author's own. [Placeholder publication.]

title: A Care Guarantee for Older Citizens
summary: Kerala is ageing faster than most of India, and many older people live without younger family nearby. Local governments are well placed to guarantee a basic level of care.
body: fellow-one Ageing Long term care Local government health-and-demography institutions-and-social-justice The problem Kerala's success in extending life expectancy and lowering fertility means that a growing share of its people are over sixty. Migration has taken many younger family members to other states and countries. The traditional assumption that older people will be cared for at home by their children no longer holds for a large number of households. Existing support, through pensions, health services and a small number of care homes, was not designed for this situation. Families who can afford it hire private caregivers, often informally. Those who cannot are left to manage alone. Principles for a response - Care close to home. Most older people want to remain in their own homes and communities. - A guaranteed minimum. Every older person who needs help with daily living should be entitled to a basic level of support, regardless of family circumstances. - Local delivery. Panchayats and municipalities already run health and welfare programs and know their residents. - Support for carers. Family members and paid caregivers need training, respite and fair conditions. Recommendations 1. Create a register of older residents who live alone or need help with daily living , maintained by each local government with consent and strict privacy safeguards. 2. Fund a basic home care entitlement , delivered through trained community caregivers, for those assessed as needing it. 3. Develop day care centres in every local government area, using existing public buildings where possible. 4. Set standards and registration for care homes and home care agencies , with regular inspection. 5. Train and certify caregivers , creating a recognised occupation with decent pay. Next steps CRGD is working with interested local governments to pilot elements of this approach and will publish the results. [Placeholder publication. Replace with real CRGD work.]

title: Kerala Needs a Fiscal Conversation, Not a Blame Game
summary: Every argument about the state's finances turns into an argument about who is to blame. The public deserves a debate about choices instead.
body: adviser-two State finances Public debate governance-finance-accountability federalism Every discussion of Kerala's public finances seems to follow the same script. The government blames the Union for reduced transfers and borrowing limits. The opposition blames the government for overspending and debt. Each side is partly right. Neither conversation helps a citizen understand the choices the state actually faces. Those choices are real and difficult. The state has commitments to its employees and pensioners that it must honour. It has public services that citizens value and expect to improve. It has infrastructure needs that will not wait. It has a population that is ageing, which will raise health and pension costs further. And it has a revenue base that, for many reasons, has not grown as fast as those commitments. A grown up conversation would start from shared facts: how much the state raises, how much it spends and on what, how much it owes and when that debt falls due. It would then ask what the options are, and who would bear the cost of each. Raise more revenue, and from whom? Spend less, and on what? Borrow more, and for what purpose? Ask more of the Union, and on what grounds? There are no painless answers. But a public that understands the choices is more likely to accept the decisions that follow, and more likely to hold its leaders to account for them. Blame is easy. Choices are harder, and they are what governing is about. The views expressed are the author's own. [Placeholder publication.]

title: The Gulf Comes Home: Return Migration and Kerala's Next Economy
summary: For half a century, work in the Gulf has shaped Kerala's households, towns and politics. As more migrants return, the state faces a question it has rarely had to answer: what will they do here?
body: associate-one scholar-two Migration Remittances Gulf Jobs employment economy strategic-affairs-and-planning Drive through almost any town in central or northern Kerala and the Gulf is visible: in the houses, the shops, the schools, the names of businesses. For two generations, work in the countries of the Gulf Cooperation Council has been the most important route to prosperity for hundreds of thousands of Kerala families. Remittances have paid for homes, education, weddings and health care. They have kept consumption high and construction busy. That story is changing. Labour policies in Gulf countries have increasingly favoured their own citizens. Wages for many semi skilled jobs have stagnated. Shocks such as the collapse in oil prices in the middle of the last decade and the pandemic sent workers home in large numbers, some for good. Younger Malayalis who migrate are increasingly choosing destinations in Europe, North America and Australia, often as students first. Who is coming back Return migrants are not one group. Some come back after decades abroad, with savings and plans to retire. Some return early because they lost their jobs, often with debts and little savings. Some come back with skills and capital and want to start a business. Others bring health problems from years of hard physical work in difficult conditions. What they share is a re entry into an economy that has changed while they were away, and a public system that was designed mainly to manage their departure, not their return. What return migrants need Our conversations with returnees, their families and support organisations suggest a consistent set of needs: - Information about jobs, schemes and opportunities, in one place and in Malayalam - Recognition of skills gained abroad, which often have no certificate that employers at home accept - Advice and credit for those who want to start enterprises, with realistic support rather than one time loans - Health care , including for chronic and occupational illness - Social security , particularly for those who return without savings Lessons from elsewhere Other countries with large migrant workforces, such as the Philippines, have built institutions specifically for returning workers, including reintegration programs, skills certification and dedicated financial products. Their experience is mixed, but it shows that return can be planned for rather than simply absorbed. A different economy The deeper question is what kind of economy can make use of the experience, savings and ambitions of returning migrants and of the young people who might otherwise leave. That is a question for the whole of Kerala's economic policy: investment, enterprise, urban development and education. Return migration is not a side issue. It is one of the clearest tests of whether the state can build an economy that does not depend on exporting its people. [Placeholder publication. This sample shows the style of a long form essay. title: Why Bus Ridership Matters More Than Metro Ridership
summary: Metro lines attract attention and investment. Buses carry far more people in Kerala, and their decline deserves at least as much concern.
body: fellow-two Public transport Buses mobility urbanisation New metro lines open with ceremony. Bus routes are cut without anyone noticing. Yet in Kerala, as in most of India, buses carry far more passengers than any rail based urban system, and they reach places metros never will. Over the past two decades, bus services in many parts of the state have declined. Operators have struggled with rising costs and fares that are politically difficult to raise. Passengers have moved to two wheelers and cars where they can afford them, adding to congestion and road danger. Those who cannot afford them, including many women, students and older people, are left with fewer and less frequent services. A metro can be a good investment in the right corridor. But a city that builds a metro while letting its bus network wither will not reduce congestion. It will simply move some of its traffic underground or overhead while the roads fill up anyway. Reversing the decline of buses would require: - dedicated space on main roads , so that buses are not stuck in the traffic they could relieve - reliable, frequent timetables , published and tracked in real time - integrated tickets across bus, metro and water transport - a sustainable financing model that recognises buses as a public service, not only a commercial operation None of this is as photogenic as a new metro station. All of it would help more people, sooner. [Placeholder publication. Replace with real CRGD commentary.]

title: Panchayat Finances After Three Decades of Decentralisation
summary: Kerala transferred real money and power to local governments in the 1990s. This report examines how local finances have evolved since, and what would strengthen them for the next thirty years.
body: scholar-one intern-one Decentralisation Local government Public finance federalism governance-finance-accountability Summary The 73rd and 74th Amendments to the Constitution, which came into force in 1993, gave panchayats and municipalities a constitutional place in Indian government. Kerala went further than most states. Through the People's Plan Campaign launched in 1996, it devolved a substantial share of the state's development budget to local governments, along with responsibility for many institutions and the staff to run them. Three decades later, this report asks how local government finances have developed, how well local governments use the resources they have, and what reforms would strengthen them. Main findings 1. Dependence on transfers remains high. Local governments raise only a modest share of their spending from their own taxes and fees. Most of their resources come from the state and from Union grants. 2. Own revenue is under exploited. Property tax assessments are often out of date, and collection efficiency varies widely between local governments of similar size. 3. Spending is constrained by timing. Funds often reach local governments late in the financial year, producing a rush to spend before the year ends. 4. Capacity is uneven. Engineering, accounting and planning staff are thinly spread, especially in smaller panchayats. 5. Accountability works best where citizens are engaged. Ward and grama sabhas that meet regularly and discuss budgets are associated with better reporting. Recommendations - Revise property tax assessments on a fixed cycle using simple, transparent methods. - Release a predictable share of devolved funds at fixed points in the year. - Create shared pools of technical staff for clusters of smaller panchayats. - Publish every local government's budget and accounts online in a standard format. - Strengthen the role of grama sabhas in reviewing spending, not only in choosing beneficiaries. Method The report draws on published budget and accounts data for local governments, documents of the State Finance Commissions, and interviews with elected representatives and officials in a sample of local governments of different sizes and regions. title: Why My Generation Is Leaving, and What Might Make Us Stay
summary: Half my class is planning to study or work abroad. A student's view of why, and of what the state could do about it.
body: intern-two Youth Migration Students abroad education employment When I ask my classmates about their plans after graduation, the answers often begin with the name of another country. For many young people in Kerala, going abroad is no longer a dream. It is the default plan. It would be easy to say this is about money. It is partly about money. But when we talk about it, the reasons are broader. We want work that matches what we studied. Many of us have seen older siblings and cousins wait years for jobs that never came, or take jobs unrelated to their degrees. We want a certain kind of life. Independence, reliable public transport, cities where you can go out in the evening, workplaces where young people are taken seriously. We want to be paid for our skills. Salaries for entry level professional jobs at home can feel very low compared with the cost of living and the cost of our education. Our friends are going. Migration builds on itself. Every person who leaves makes it easier for the next. What might make us stay? Not speeches about loyalty to the homeland. Jobs in the kinds of work we trained for. Cities that are pleasant to live in. A start up culture that forgives failure. A sense that young people can shape decisions, not just wait for them. Many of us would like to stay, or to come back. Give us a reason. This piece was written as part of the Young Thoughts mentoring program. Views are the author's own. [Placeholder publication.]

title: Five Steps Towards Halving Road Deaths
summary: Road crashes kill and injure thousands of people in Kerala every year, most of them pedestrians, cyclists and riders of two wheelers. Proven measures exist. This brief sets out five.
body: fellow-two Road safety Transport mobility The problem Road crashes are among the leading causes of death for young people in India, and Kerala's dense, mixed traffic makes its roads particularly dangerous for those outside cars: people walking, cycling and riding two wheelers. Behind every death are families who lose an earner, a child or a parent. Countries and cities that have sharply reduced road deaths did not do so through public awareness campaigns alone. They changed the design of roads, the speed of traffic and the way crashes are investigated. Five steps 1. Manage speed where people are. Lower and enforce speed limits near schools, markets, hospitals and junctions, with physical measures such as raised crossings rather than signs alone. 2. Fix the most dangerous places first. Use crash data to identify the stretches and junctions where most deaths occur, and redesign them within a fixed time. 3. Build for people on foot. Continuous footpaths, safe crossings and street lighting on every road where people walk. 4. Investigate every fatal crash for its causes , not only to assign blame, and publish what is learned. 5. Treat the first hour. Strengthen emergency response so that injured people reach trauma care quickly. Making it happen These steps need a lead agency with authority and a budget, clear annual targets, and public reporting on progress. Road safety is a responsibility shared by transport, public works, police, health and local governments. Without someone in charge, it will remain everyone's concern and no one's job. title: Women's Work Is Kerala's Missing Growth Engine
summary: A state that educates its daughters as well as Kerala does, and then loses their talent to the labour market, is leaving its most important growth opportunity unused.
body: fellow-one Women and work Economic growth employment economy institutions-and-social-justice Kerala has done what many societies still struggle to do. It has educated its girls as well as its boys, and its young women now outnumber young men in many university courses. Yet when education ends, a large proportion of these women do not enter paid work, or leave it after marriage or the birth of a child. This is often discussed as a social question. It is also an economic one. An economy that leaves a large share of its most educated people out of the workforce is growing more slowly than it could. Every woman who wants to work but cannot is a loss to her family, to employers and to the public revenue that her earnings would generate. The reasons are not mysterious. Women in Kerala, like women across India, do most of the unpaid care work in their households. Safe, reliable transport is scarce in many places. Childcare is expensive or unavailable. Many jobs that match women's qualifications are located far from home. Social expectations still discourage many women from working after marriage. Each of these barriers can be lowered by policy: public childcare, safe transport, flexible and remote work, enforcement of workplace protections, and, above all, more jobs of the kind educated women want, close to where they live. The state's development has been built on investing in people. The next phase should make sure that investment is not wasted. The views expressed are the author's own. [Placeholder publication.]

title: After the Landslides: Building Safer Hill Communities
summary: Landslides in Kerala's hill districts have taken many lives in recent years. This special report brings together geology, land use, local governance and the experience of survivors to set out how hill communities can be made safer.
body: researcher-three scholar-three fellow-two Landslides Disaster preparedness Western Ghats Land use environment-and-disaster-management urbanisation agriculture-and-rural-development Why this report The landslides that struck parts of Wayanad in July 2024 were among the deadliest disasters in Kerala's recent history, and they followed other serious landslides in the hill districts in earlier monsoons. Each event prompted grief, relief efforts and promises of change. This report asks what has actually changed, and what still needs to. It draws together the work of three CRGD research verticals: Environment and Disaster Management, Urbanisation, and Agriculture and Rural Development. Structure of the report 1. Understanding the hazard. What makes slopes in the Western Ghats unstable, and how intense rainfall, soil, geology and human modification interact. 2. Who lives in harm's way. How settlements, plantations and infrastructure have grown on and below vulnerable slopes, and why. 3. Warning and evacuation. How early warning systems work, where they have succeeded and where they have failed. 4. Rebuilding. The choices facing families and governments after a disaster: where to rebuild, how, and with what support. 5. Governing land use. The laws and plans that regulate construction and quarrying on slopes, and their enforcement. 6. Voices from affected communities. What survivors, local officials and volunteers say they need. Key recommendations - Produce and publish detailed landslide susceptibility maps at the level of local government wards. - Tie rainfall based warnings to clear, pre agreed evacuation triggers at the community level. - Require geological assessment before significant construction on slopes above a defined gradient. - Give displaced families real choice in rehabilitation, with livelihood support as well as housing. - Train and equip local volunteers, who are always the first responders. title: The Sea Wall and the Shore
summary: Along much of Kerala's coast, homes, roads and boats face the sea with less beach every year. The responses chosen now will shape the coast for a century.
body: scholar-two researcher-three Coastal erosion Fishing communities Climate adaptation maritime-economy environment-and-disaster-management The fishing villages of Kerala's coast have always lived with the sea's moods: the monsoon swell, the shifting sand, the seasons when boats cannot go out. What is new is the scale and persistence of erosion in many places, and the sense among coastal residents that the shore is retreating faster than it can be defended. Why the shore is moving Beaches are not fixed. Sand moves along the coast with waves and currents, building up in some places and wearing away in others. Human structures change these flows. Harbours, breakwaters, groynes and sea walls can protect one stretch of coast while starving the next of sand. Sand mining in rivers reduces the sediment that reaches the sea. Rising sea levels and changing wave patterns add further pressure. The limits of walls The most common response to erosion has been to build sea walls of granite boulders. Walls can protect property in the short term, but they often cause the beach in front of them to disappear, leaving no place to land a boat or dry a net. They need constant maintenance and can fail in severe storms. Engineers and ecologists increasingly recommend a mix of approaches: beach nourishment, offshore reefs, restoration of dunes and coastal vegetation, and, in some places, planned retreat from the most vulnerable stretches. None of these is simple, cheap or uncontroversial. Whose decision Coastal decisions are often made by engineering departments, with limited involvement of the people whose homes and livelihoods are at stake. Fishing communities have deep knowledge of the coast, but they are rarely asked. Rehabilitation schemes that move families inland can protect lives but separate fishers from the sea that sustains them. What a better process would look like - Coastal plans for whole sediment cells , not single villages, so that protecting one place does not damage another - Independent assessment of proposed structures before they are built - Consultation with fishing communities at every stage, with their knowledge treated as evidence - Choice and dignity in relocation , with housing close to the coast and support for livelihoods The coast that Kerala's grandchildren inherit will be shaped by decisions made in the next few years. They deserve to be made with care. [Placeholder publication. Replace with real CRGD work.]

title: Explainer: How the Finance Commission Shares Tax Revenue Among States
summary: Every five years, a commission decides how a large share of India's tax revenue is divided between the Union and the states, and among the states. Here is how it works.
body: scholar-one Finance Commission Fiscal federalism Explainer federalism governance-finance-accountability What is the Finance Commission? The Finance Commission is a constitutional body set up by the President under Article 280 of the Constitution, normally every five years. Its main task is to recommend how the net proceeds of taxes collected by the Union should be shared between the Union and the states, and how the states' share should be divided among them. Two decisions The Commission makes two kinds of decision: 1. Vertical sharing. What share of the divisible pool of central taxes goes to the states as a whole. The Fourteenth Finance Commission raised this share to 42 per cent; the Fifteenth set it at 41 per cent after the reorganisation of Jammu and Kashmir. 2. Horizontal sharing. How the states' share is divided among individual states. This is done using a formula with several criteria, each given a weight. The formula The Fifteenth Finance Commission used these criteria: Criterion What it measures Weight --- --- --- Income distance How far a state's per capita income is below that of the richest states 45% Population Population in the 2011 Census 15% Area Geographical area 15% Forest and ecology Share of dense forest 10% Demographic performance Success in reducing fertility 12.5% Tax and fiscal effort Efficiency in collecting own taxes 2.5% Why it matters to Kerala Criteria such as income distance favour poorer states, which is the purpose of redistribution. States like Kerala, with higher incomes and early success in reducing population growth, have argued that some criteria penalise them. The demographic performance criterion was introduced partly in response to such concerns. Grants Besides tax sharing, the Commission recommends grants, for example to local governments, for disaster management, and to states whose revenue falls short of their needs. What next The Sixteenth Finance Commission's recommendations cover the five years from 2026 to 2031. CRGD will publish an analysis of what they mean for Kerala. [Placeholder publication. title: From Classroom to Career: Graduate Employability in Kerala
summary: Kerala educates its young people to a high level, yet many graduates struggle to find work that matches their qualifications. This report traces the gap between what colleges teach and what employers need.
body: researcher-one associate-one Higher education Youth unemployment Skills education employment Summary A degree has long been the expected path to a secure future for young people in Kerala. Yet graduates in the state face some of the highest rates of unemployment among educated youth in India, while employers report that they cannot find candidates with the skills they need. This report asks why. What we examined - the courses students choose, and why they choose them - what employers in growing sectors say they look for - how colleges connect, or fail to connect, with employers - the role of competitive examinations for public sector jobs in shaping student choices - the experience of young women graduates in particular Main themes Waiting for the right job. Many graduates spend years preparing for public sector recruitment examinations, which offer security and status but very few places. Skills that are not taught. Employers emphasise communication, problem solving and practical experience. Most courses focus on examinations. Weak bridges. Internships, apprenticeships and placement services are limited in many colleges. Women's choices constrained. Concerns about travel, safety, working hours and family expectations narrow the jobs that many women graduates feel able to take. Recommendations 1. Make a supervised internship part of every undergraduate degree. 2. Fund career guidance in every college, staffed by trained counsellors. 3. Support colleges to design short skill modules with local employers. 4. Publish employment outcomes for every course and college, so that students can choose with better information. 5. Address safe transport and childcare as part of employment policy for women. [Placeholder publication. Replace with real CRGD work.]

title: How We Choose Our Research Questions
summary: There are far more important questions than any institution can answer. A note on how CRGD decides what to work on, and how you can suggest a question.
body: scholar-one Research methods About CRGD state-and-politics One of the hardest decisions a research institution makes is what not to study. Every week we hear of problems that deserve attention. Our capacity is limited, and a half finished study helps no one. So we use a few simple tests. Does someone need the answer? We prefer questions that a decision maker, an institution or a community is actually facing, where better evidence could change what they do. Can we add something? If good research already exists, our job may be to bring it to the right people rather than to repeat it. We look for gaps. Can we do it well? We ask whether we have, or can bring in, the skills and access the question requires. Is the timing right? Some questions are urgent because a decision is about to be made. Others are slow and structural. We try to keep a balance between the two. Will it be heard? A study that no one will read is a poor use of time. We think about who the audience is from the start. Questions that pass these tests go to the relevant research vertical, which keeps a short list of priorities published on its page. We welcome suggestions. Some of our best projects began with a message from a reader, an official or a student. If you have a question you think we should be asking, tell us. [Placeholder publication.]

title: What the Data Can and Cannot Tell Us About Women's Work
summary: Headlines about women's employment often rest on surveys that count some kinds of work and miss others. A guide to reading the numbers carefully.
body: associate-one Women and work Labour statistics Data employment institutions-and-social-justice Few statistics are cited more often in debates about Kerala's development than the share of women in paid work. It is usually presented as a paradox: a state with highly educated women in which comparatively few are counted as employed. Before drawing conclusions, it is worth understanding how the numbers are produced. How work is measured India's main source on employment is the Periodic Labour Force Survey, run by the National Statistical Office. It classifies people by their activity status over a reference period. Definitions matter: whether a woman who helps in a family business, keeps livestock or does piece work at home is counted as working depends on how the question is asked and answered. Common pitfalls - Comparing different definitions. Rates based on "usual status" and "current weekly status" are not interchangeable. - Ignoring age groups. Rising enrolment in higher education lowers participation among young women, which is not a bad thing in itself. - Missing unpaid work. Care and household work, done mostly by women, is not counted as employment in labour force statistics, though time use surveys measure it. - Over reading small changes. Year to year changes at the state level can fall within the margin of sampling error. Better questions Rather than asking only how many women work, policy makers might ask: - What kinds of work do educated women want, and where is it available? - How do travel time, safety and childcare affect their choices? - How much unpaid care work are women doing, and who could share it? These questions require more than a single headline rate. They are the ones that lead to useful policy. [Placeholder publication. Replace with real CRGD work.]

title: Explainer: What Does a Panchayat Actually Do?
summary: Panchayats run schools, health centres, roads and welfare programs in your neighbourhood. A plain language guide to what they do and how you can take part.
body: researcher-one Local government Panchayat Explainer federalism governance-finance-accountability Three tiers Rural Kerala is governed locally by three tiers of panchayats: - Grama panchayats at the village level, closest to residents - Block panchayats covering several grama panchayats - District panchayats covering the whole district Towns and cities are governed by municipalities and municipal corporations . Where the powers come from The 73rd Amendment to the Constitution, in force since 1993, made panchayats a constitutional tier of government and listed 29 subjects in the Eleventh Schedule that states may devolve to them. Kerala's Panchayat Raj Act, 1994, set out their powers in the state, and the People's Plan Campaign from 1996 transferred substantial funds and responsibilities to them. What a grama panchayat does Depending on the subject, a grama panchayat may: - maintain village roads, street lights and public spaces - run or support anganwadis, primary schools and primary health institutions transferred to it - manage drinking water schemes and waste collection - select beneficiaries for housing and welfare schemes - prepare an annual development plan and budget - issue certificates and licences How to take part Every ward has a grama sabha , a meeting of all registered voters in the ward, which must be held regularly. The grama sabha discusses the development plan, reviews spending and selects beneficiaries for schemes. It is one of the most direct forms of democracy in India, and it works best when residents attend. Where to find information Panchayats publish their plans, budgets and beneficiary lists. You can also ask for information under the Right to Information Act, 2005. [Placeholder publication. Replace with real CRGD work.]

title: What a Mock Assembly Taught Me About Real Democracy
summary: A day spent debating a bill as a pretend legislator changed how one student thinks about politics.
body: intern-one Campus clubs Democracy Youth state-and-politics I signed up for our policy club's mock assembly because a friend asked me to. I expected a debating competition. What I got was a lesson in how difficult it is to make a law. We were given a draft bill on regulating private coaching centres, and divided into a ruling coalition, an opposition and a group of independent members. We had a morning to read the bill and an afternoon to debate, amend and vote on it. The first surprise was how much detail mattered. A single definition, of what counts as a coaching centre, decided who would be covered and who would not. We spent an hour on it. The second surprise was how much I changed my mind. I began firmly in favour of strict regulation. By the end, after hearing from members playing small teachers and parents in rural areas, I voted for a much lighter version. The third surprise was how hard compromise is when your side expects you to win. Members who negotiated with the other side were accused of betrayal by their own. I came away with more respect for legislators, and more impatience with legislatures that pass laws without this kind of debate. I also came away wanting to do it again. This piece was written as part of the Young Thoughts mentoring program. Views are the author's own. [Placeholder publication.]

title: Five Questions to Ask of Any State Budget
summary: Budget speeches are full of announcements. The numbers tell a quieter story. Here are five questions that reveal what a budget actually commits the state to.
body: scholar-one Budget State finances Public expenditure governance-finance-accountability Every year the budget speech dominates the news for a day. New schemes are announced, allocations are praised or criticised, and then attention moves on. The documents that accompany the speech, often running to thousands of pages, receive much less attention. They contain the answers to five questions that matter more than any announcement. 1. How much of the revenue is already spoken for? Look at committed expenditure : salaries, pensions and interest payments. When these absorb most of the state's revenue receipts, there is little room for new priorities, whatever the speech says. Track this share over several years. 2. Is the state borrowing to invest or to pay bills? Compare the revenue deficit with the fiscal deficit . Borrowing to build assets that will serve future generations is defensible. Borrowing to meet day to day expenses passes the bill to the future without leaving anything behind. 3. What happened to last year's promises? Compare last year's budget estimates with the revised estimates and, when they are available, the actuals . Large gaps, especially in capital spending, show where announcements were not followed by action. 4. Where is the money going, not just how much? Look beyond totals to the composition of spending within departments. A larger health budget may be mostly salaries, or mostly new buildings, or mostly medicines. Each tells a different story. 5. What is outside the budget? Find the statements on guarantees and on borrowing by state owned bodies . These obligations may not appear in the headline deficit but can fall on the budget in future. Using these questions None of these questions requires specialist training. They require time and patience with the budget documents, which are published online. CRGD publishes a plain language reading of the state budget every year that works through these questions. [Placeholder publication. Replace with real CRGD work.]

title: Review: Reading the State's Annual Economic Review
summary: Each year the State Planning Board publishes a detailed review of the economy alongside the budget. It is the most useful document few people read. A guide to its strengths and gaps.
body: contributor-two Review Economic data economy governance-finance-accountability Every year, the Kerala State Planning Board publishes the Economic Review , a comprehensive account of the state's economy, presented to the legislature with the budget. It runs to hundreds of pages, covering everything from agriculture and industry to health, education, local government and the environment. Its strengths Breadth. Few documents bring together so much information about the state in one place. For anyone starting research on a Kerala policy question, it is the first place to look. Consistency. Because it appears every year in a broadly similar structure, it allows comparison over time. Department data. It includes data supplied by government departments that is not always published elsewhere. Its limitations Description more than analysis. The review reports what happened more than it explains why, and rarely evaluates whether programs achieved their aims. Data access. Much of the data appears in tables within the document. Publishing the underlying data in machine readable form would make it far more useful to researchers and journalists. Timing. Some figures necessarily lag by a year or more. How to use it Read the review alongside the budget documents and, where possible, the reports of the Comptroller and Auditor General. Use it as a map of what is known, and a guide to the questions that need asking. [Placeholder publication. Replace with real CRGD review.]

Beyond academia, Dr. Mirza contributes opinion pieces and columns to leading newspapers in multiple languages and is actively involved in cultural, literary, and artistic forums.
