title: Governance, Finance and Accountability
summary: How governments raise and spend public money, how they are held to account for it, and how the machinery of administration can serve citizens better.
body: State finances and budgets Public expenditure quality Audit and oversight Administrative reform Local government finance Transparency and right to information What does the state actually get for each rupee it spends on salaries, pensions, subsidies and capital works? How can off budget borrowing be made transparent without stopping investment the state needs? Which reports of the Comptroller and Auditor General lead to action, and why do others not? How much real fiscal freedom do panchayats and municipalities have, and how well do they use it? Every policy promise eventually becomes a line in a budget. This vertical follows the money: where it comes from, where it goes, and whether anyone can tell what it achieved. Why it matters Kerala built strong public services on the back of steady public spending, but a large share of today's revenue is committed before the year begins, to salaries, pensions and interest. Choices about capital investment, welfare and debt now carry consequences for decades. Citizens and legislators deserve clear, independent analysis of those choices, not slogans from either side. Accountability is the other half of the story. Audit reports, legislative committees, the right to information and social audits all exist on paper. The question this vertical asks is how well they work in practice, and what would make them work better. How we work - Budget analysis. Each year we publish a plain language reading of the Kerala budget and of relevant Union budget decisions within weeks of their presentation. - Follow the audit. We track selected audit findings over time to see which are acted upon. - Local finance. With partner panchayats and municipalities, we study how decentralised planning funds are planned, spent and reported. - Administrative reform. We document reforms that worked elsewhere in India and abroad, and test whether they would travel. The vertical works closely with the Federalism, Economy and Institutions and Social Justice verticals.

title: Education
summary: From early childhood to university, how Kerala and India can move from near universal access to genuinely good learning for every student.
body: School learning outcomes Higher education governance Teacher preparation Students who study abroad Skills and employability Inclusive education Now that almost every child is in school, what do they actually learn, and how do we know? Why do so many young people leave Kerala to study, and what would make them stay or return? How should public universities be governed so that they are both autonomous and accountable? What does it take to make children with disabilities full participants in ordinary classrooms? Kerala's achievement in literacy and school enrolment is part of its public identity. The harder question now is quality: whether schools and colleges equip young people to think, to work and to take part in public life. Why it matters Access is no longer the main problem. Learning levels, the relevance of degrees to the jobs that exist, the governance of universities, and the steady movement of students abroad are. Each of these is a policy problem with consequences for the economy and for families who invest heavily in education. How we work - Evidence on learning. We analyse national and state assessment data, and run small field studies to understand what is happening inside classrooms. - University governance. We compare how universities in India and elsewhere are funded, led and held to account. - Student journeys. We study why students choose the courses and places they do, including the growing number who go overseas. - Inclusion. We look at how children with disabilities, children of migrant workers and first generation learners are served. Findings are shared with teachers, school leaders, university administrators and the education department, and with parents through plain language explainers.

title: Health and Demography
summary: How a society that has largely won the battles against early death and high fertility can meet its next challenges, from chronic disease to an ageing population.
body: Primary health care Non communicable diseases Ageing and care Health financing Epidemic preparedness Mental health How should primary care change when most of the disease burden is chronic rather than infectious? Who will care for older people in households where the young have migrated? How much do families still pay out of pocket for care, and for what? What did recent outbreaks teach the state about surveillance and response, and has it been learned? Kerala's health and demographic record is often cited as a model for the developing world: long life expectancy, low infant mortality and low fertility. That success has produced a new set of problems that the existing system was not designed for. Why it matters Diabetes, hypertension, cancer and mental illness now account for most ill health. The population is ageing faster than in most of India, and many older people live without working age children nearby. Families still pay a significant share of health costs themselves. Meanwhile, the state has had to respond to outbreaks of new and returning infections. Each of these demands decisions about money, staff and institutions. How we work - Primary care. We study how family health centres and community health workers are adapting to chronic disease care. - Ageing. We examine pensions, long term care, elder abuse and the role of local governments in caring for older citizens. - Health spending. We track public health budgets and the cost of care to households. - Preparedness. We document how outbreaks were handled and what systems remain in place for the next one. The vertical draws on demographers, doctors, economists and social workers, and works with the Employment and Economy verticals on migration and its effect on families.

title: Employment
summary: Why educated young people struggle to find work at home, why women's participation in paid work remains low, and how migration in and out of Kerala shapes the labour market.
body: Youth and graduate unemployment Women and paid work Gulf migration and return Inter-state migrant workers Gig and platform work Labour law and social security Why does a highly educated workforce face unemployment at home while employers report shortages? What keeps educated women out of paid work, and which policies have changed that elsewhere? How should the state prepare for workers returning from the Gulf? What protections do workers from other states actually receive in Kerala? Work is where public policy meets private life most directly. This vertical studies who works, who does not, and why, with a particular focus on the paradoxes of the Kerala labour market. Why it matters Kerala sends hundreds of thousands of its own people abroad to work, while depending on workers from other states for construction, hospitality and agriculture at home. It educates its young women to a high level, yet relatively few of them are in paid employment. Graduates queue for government jobs while private employers say they cannot find the skills they need. None of these patterns is inevitable. All of them have policy causes and policy remedies. How we work - Labour market analysis. We read national surveys closely for what they say about Kerala and comparable states. - Migration studies. We follow emigrant, returning and incoming workers, with attention to families left behind. - Women and work. We study barriers such as mobility, care work, social norms and workplace safety. - New forms of work. We examine platform work, self employment and the reach of social security. The vertical collaborates with trade unions, employers' associations, migrant support groups and the labour department.

title: Federalism
summary: How powers, money and responsibilities are shared between the Union, the states and local governments, and how that balance affects what Kerala can do for its people.
body: Fiscal federalism and Finance Commissions Goods and Services Tax Centrally sponsored schemes Borrowing limits Decentralisation to local bodies Inter-state cooperation Do the formulas used to share central taxes treat states that controlled population growth fairly? How has the Goods and Services Tax changed the fiscal autonomy of states? When the Union funds a scheme and a state runs it, who is accountable for the results? How can the constitutional promise of strong local government be completed? India's Constitution divides power between the Union and the states, and since 1992 has given a constitutional place to panchayats and municipalities. How that division works in practice is one of the most consequential and least understood questions in Indian public life. Why it matters Kerala raises a large share of its own revenue but depends on transfers for much of the rest. The rules for those transfers, the design of the Goods and Services Tax, conditions attached to central schemes and limits on state borrowing all shape what the state government can do. Kerala is also known for decentralising real power and money to local governments, an experiment that offers lessons and unfinished business. How we work - Finance Commission analysis. We study each Finance Commission's terms of reference, the submissions made to it and the outcome for states. - GST monitoring. We follow revenue trends, compensation issues and decisions of the GST Council. - Scheme design. We look at how centrally sponsored schemes are funded and implemented at state and local levels. - Local democracy. We study the functioning of panchayats and municipalities, their finances and their planning. We aim to be useful to all sides of a debate that is often conducted in partisan terms. Our analysis is evidence first, and we publish our data so others can test it.

title: Tourism and Culture
summary: How tourism and cultural life can bring prosperity to communities without eroding the places, traditions and environments that attract visitors in the first place.
body: Responsible and community tourism Heritage conservation Arts and the creative economy Ayurveda and wellness tourism Carrying capacity of fragile places Cultural institutions Who earns the money that tourists spend, and how much stays in local communities? How many visitors can a hill station, a beach or a backwater sustain? How should public funds support artists, performers and cultural institutions? What does good heritage conservation look like in a living town? Tourism is one of Kerala's most visible industries, and culture is one of its deepest sources of identity. This vertical studies both as matters of public policy: who benefits, who bears the costs and how the long term can be protected. Why it matters Tourism supports many livelihoods, from homestays and boatmen to performers and craftspeople. It can also crowd out residents, strain water and waste systems, and damage the landscapes that bring visitors. Kerala has experimented with responsible tourism models that link visitors to local producers. Culture, from classical and folk arts to literature and cinema, needs public support that respects artistic freedom. How we work - Destination studies. We study specific destinations to understand visitor numbers, local incomes and environmental pressure. - Community tourism. We evaluate models that aim to share tourism income more widely. - Cultural policy. We examine public funding for the arts, cultural institutions and heritage sites. - Recovery and resilience. We look at how tourism communities recover from floods, landslides and pandemics. This vertical works closely with the Environment and Disaster Management and Urbanisation verticals.

title: Mobility
summary: How people and goods move across a densely settled state, and how transport policy can make journeys safer, cleaner, fairer and quicker.
body: Public transport and buses Rail and metro systems Road safety Walking and cycling Electric mobility Freight and logistics Why has public bus use declined, and what would bring passengers back? Which large transport projects are worth their cost, and how should that be judged? What would it take to halve road deaths in Kerala? How should streets be redesigned for the people who walk on them? Kerala's settlements run almost continuously along its coast and midlands, which makes transport both essential and difficult. Roads are crowded, private vehicle ownership has grown quickly and road safety remains a serious concern. Why it matters Transport decisions shape where people can live and work, how much time they lose to travel, what they breathe and whether they arrive safely. Large projects such as metro lines, highways and proposed rail corridors involve heavy public investment and often provoke strong disagreement. Smaller decisions, such as bus routes, footpaths and junction design, affect more people every day. How we work - Project appraisal. We review the economic, social and environmental case for major transport investments, using published data. - Public transport. We study the finances and services of public bus operators and metro systems. - Road safety. We analyse crash data and the effectiveness of enforcement, engineering and education. - Active travel. We document how streets work for pedestrians, cyclists, children and older people. The vertical works with the Urbanisation and Environment verticals and with transport user groups.

title: Agriculture and Rural Development
summary: The future of farming and rural livelihoods in a state where land is scarce, labour is costly and the climate is changing.
body: Paddy and wetland conservation Plantation crops and prices Food security and the public distribution system Farmer collectives Livestock and fisheries inland Women's collectives and rural enterprise Can paddy cultivation be made viable without losing wetlands to other uses? How should rubber, spice, tea and coffee growers be protected from price shocks? What role can farmer producer organisations and women's collectives play in rural incomes? How should the public distribution system change as diets and incomes change? Agriculture's share of Kerala's economy has fallen, but farming and rural livelihoods remain central to food security, ecology and the incomes of many households. Why it matters Paddy land has been converted to other uses for decades, with consequences for water and food. Plantation farmers are exposed to international prices they cannot control. Agricultural labour is expensive and scarce. Climate change is altering rainfall and pests. At the same time, women's collectives and farmer groups have shown that rural enterprise can work at scale. How we work - Land and water. We study the implementation of laws that protect paddy land and wetlands, and their effects on farmers. - Prices and markets. We follow commodity prices, procurement and support schemes for key crops. - Collectives. We evaluate farmer producer organisations and women's self help networks. - Food policy. We analyse the public distribution system and nutrition programs. The vertical works with the Environment, Employment and Economy verticals, and with farmer organisations and agricultural universities.

title: Strategic Affairs and Planning
summary: Long range planning for the state, and the strategic questions of security, diaspora and the Indian Ocean that matter to Kerala and to India.
body: State planning and foresight Coastal and maritime security Diaspora and the Gulf Indian Ocean region Energy and supply chain security Scenario planning What should the state plan for over the next twenty five years, and who should do the planning? How do events in the Gulf affect households, remittances and the state economy? What does Kerala's position on the Indian Ocean mean for trade and security? How can government build the habit of planning for shocks before they arrive? Kerala is one of the few states that has kept a strong planning tradition after the national Planning Commission was replaced. This vertical asks how long term planning can be done well, and looks outward to the strategic questions that shape the state's future. Why it matters Few states are as exposed to events abroad as Kerala. Conflict or recession in the Gulf affects jobs and remittances within weeks. The state's long coastline makes maritime trade and coastal security matters of direct concern. Decisions about energy, ports and technology have strategic dimensions. Good planning means preparing for these possibilities rather than reacting to them. How we work - Foresight. We use scenario methods to explore possible futures for the state economy and society. - Diaspora. We study the links between Keralites abroad and the state, including investment, philanthropy and return. - Maritime and regional affairs. We follow developments in the Indian Ocean region that affect the state. - Planning practice. We study how plans are prepared, monitored and revised. The vertical works closely with the Maritime Economy and Economy verticals.

title: Science, Energy, Fintech and AI
summary: How science, technology, clean energy and artificial intelligence can serve the public, and how they should be governed.
body: Artificial intelligence in government Digital public infrastructure Data protection and privacy Renewable energy and the grid Startups and innovation policy Science funding and research institutions Where can artificial intelligence improve public services, and where should it not be used at all? How should government protect citizens' data while using it to plan better? How fast can the state move to clean power, and who pays for the transition? What makes an innovation ecosystem produce lasting firms rather than short lived ones? Technology is changing how governments work, how people earn and how energy is produced. This vertical studies those changes with a public interest lens: what helps citizens, what harms them, and what rules are needed. Why it matters Kerala was early to build technology parks, digital literacy programs and public internet infrastructure. Government departments are now experimenting with automated systems and artificial intelligence. At the same time, the state depends heavily on electricity bought from outside and faces choices about solar, storage and grid investment. Each of these areas needs informed public debate. How we work - AI and public services. We study real deployments of automated decision making in Indian governments and propose safeguards. - Digital rights. We analyse data protection law and its implementation. - Energy transition. We examine power purchase, rooftop solar, storage and tariffs. - Innovation policy. We look at what public support for startups and research institutions achieves. The vertical brings together engineers, lawyers, economists and social scientists.

title: Maritime Economy
summary: Ports, shipping, fisheries and coastal communities, and how Kerala can build a maritime economy that is prosperous, fair and sustainable.
body: Ports and transhipment Fisheries and fishing communities Coastal erosion and protection Shipbuilding and repair Coastal tourism Marine ecology What will a deep water transhipment port mean for Thiruvananthapuram's economy, and for the coast around it? How can traditional fishing communities share in the growth of the maritime economy? Which approaches to coastal erosion work, and which make it worse? How should fish stocks be managed so that they last? Kerala has a long coastline, a major port at Kochi, a new deep water transhipment port at Vizhinjam near Thiruvananthapuram, and fishing communities whose history goes back centuries. The maritime economy is one of the state's largest opportunities and most delicate balancing acts. Why it matters Port led growth can bring investment, logistics and jobs. It can also change shorelines, displace livelihoods and strain infrastructure. Fishing communities face declining catches, coastal erosion, and exclusion from decisions that affect them. Getting the balance right requires evidence, consultation and long term thinking. How we work - Ports and logistics. We study how ports are connected to the wider economy and what policies help local enterprise benefit. - Fishing communities. We work with fishing communities to document livelihoods, risks and priorities. - Coastal change. We review evidence on erosion, sea walls and nature based alternatives. - Blue economy. We examine marine tourism, aquaculture and shipbuilding. The vertical works with the Strategic Affairs and Planning and Environment verticals. Being based in Thiruvananthapuram, CRGD is close to the coast it studies.

title: Society, Law and Policy
summary: How laws are made, interpreted and enforced, and how they meet the realities of social life, from family and religion to speech and policing.
body: Legislative quality Courts and access to justice Policing and criminal justice Free speech and media regulation Family law and gender Social norms and change How carefully are new laws drafted, debated and reviewed before they pass? What stands between an ordinary citizen and timely justice? How should the state respond to online harms without restricting legitimate speech? Which reforms in policing have improved trust and outcomes? Laws express a society's intentions. Whether they work depends on how they are drafted, how institutions apply them and how people experience them. This vertical studies that whole journey. Why it matters Legislatures pass laws quickly and sometimes with little debate. Courts carry large backlogs. Policing affects public trust in the state more than almost any other service. New questions about online speech, privacy and misinformation are reaching legislatures and courts faster than evidence about them. Each of these is a question of law and of society at once. How we work - Legislative scrutiny. We analyse bills and ordinances, and the debates around them. - Access to justice. We study legal aid, alternative dispute resolution and court delays. - Rights and liberties. We follow developments in speech, privacy and policing. - Social research. We use surveys and interviews to understand how laws are experienced. Lawyers, sociologists and political scientists work together in this vertical, which collaborates closely with Institutions and Social Justice.

title: Institutions and Social Justice
summary: Whether public institutions treat every citizen fairly, and how policy can close the gaps that caste, gender, disability, tribe and poverty still produce.
body: Caste and affirmative action Adivasi communities Gender equality Disability rights Welfare delivery Independent oversight bodies Which groups have been left behind by Kerala's development, and why? How well do commissions, ombudsmen and tribunals protect citizens' rights? What do welfare schemes look like from the point of view of the people meant to receive them? How can public institutions become accessible to persons with disabilities in practice, not just on paper? Kerala's social development is impressive in averages, but averages can hide persistent gaps. Adivasi communities, Dalit households, fishing communities, persons with disabilities and many women experience a very different state from the one described in headline figures. Why it matters The legitimacy of public institutions rests on fair treatment. Independent bodies such as human rights commissions, the Lok Ayukta, information commissions and commissions for specific communities exist to protect citizens. Welfare programs exist to support those with least. Whether they work as intended is a matter of evidence, and of justice. How we work - Gap analysis. We use data to identify where outcomes differ between groups and regions. - Institutional review. We study the work of oversight and rights bodies. - Listening studies. We document the experience of people using welfare and public services. - Inclusion audits. We help public bodies assess their accessibility and fairness. The vertical works in partnership with community organisations and with the Society, Law and Policy vertical.

title: Economy
summary: The structure and prospects of Kerala's economy, and how growth can create good jobs, public revenue and broad prosperity.
body: Growth and structural change Remittances and consumption Investment climate Small and medium enterprises Industrial policy Prices and household welfare What will drive Kerala's growth over the next decade as remittances change? Why does the state attract less private investment than its human capital would suggest? What do small firms need most from government? How do national economic decisions show up in Kerala household budgets? Kerala's economy has long followed its own path: strong services, high consumption, large remittance inflows and a modest industrial base. This vertical studies how that model is changing and what policy can do to secure the next phase of growth. Why it matters Remittances have supported household consumption and construction for decades, but the pattern of migration is changing. The state needs investment that creates jobs suited to its educated workforce, and revenue to sustain its public services. Small and medium enterprises employ many people but struggle with credit, regulation and markets. How we work - Economic monitoring. We publish regular notes on the state economy using official data. - Enterprise studies. We survey firms to understand what helps and hinders them. - Investment climate. We compare regulatory processes with other states. - Household economics. We study how prices, credit and income affect families. The vertical works closely with Governance, Finance and Accountability, Employment and Maritime Economy.

title: Environment and Disaster Management
summary: Protecting the ecology of the Western Ghats, the coast and the wetlands, and preparing communities for floods, landslides and a changing climate.
body: Floods and landslides Western Ghats ecology Climate adaptation Waste management Wetlands and water Disaster governance What has changed in disaster preparedness since the floods of 2018? How should land use be regulated on slopes known to be unstable? What would a credible climate adaptation plan for a coastal district contain? Why do waste management systems fail, and what makes some succeed? Kerala's environment is extraordinarily rich and increasingly fragile. Floods, landslides, coastal erosion and extreme heat have shown how quickly natural hazards become human disasters when land use, infrastructure and preparedness fall short. Why it matters The floods of 2018 and the landslides that have since devastated hill communities changed public understanding of risk in the state. Decisions about quarrying, construction on slopes, wetland conversion and river management are environmental decisions and disaster decisions at once. Climate change raises the stakes further. How we work - Risk mapping. We combine public data on hazards with information about settlements and livelihoods. - Preparedness reviews. We study how early warning, evacuation and relief systems performed in past events. - Ecological policy. We follow regulation of the Western Ghats, wetlands and coastal zones. - Waste and pollution. We study waste systems in towns and panchayats. The vertical works with local governments, scientists, civil defence volunteers and affected communities.

title: Gender, State and Politics
summary: How the state is governed in practice: the legislature, the executive, political parties and the political culture that shapes public decisions.
body: Functioning of the legislature Coalition politics Political parties and organisation Civil service and the executive Public opinion Comparative state politics How much time does the legislature spend scrutinising laws and budgets, and how could it spend more? How do coalitions shape the policies that governments adopt? What is the relationship between political parties and civil society organisations? How does Kerala's political culture compare with that of other states? Kerala's politics is intensely participatory, closely contested and often polarised. This vertical studies the institutions and practices of government and politics with the same evidence based approach CRGD applies to policy. Why it matters Policy outcomes depend on how governments are formed, how legislatures function and how parties compete. Strong scrutiny of the executive improves decisions. Weak scrutiny allows mistakes to go unchallenged. Understanding the political system is essential for anyone who wants to change policy. How we work - Legislative monitoring. We track sittings, debates, questions and committee work in the state assembly. - Comparative analysis. We compare institutions and practices across Indian states. - Political history. We document how key policies were made, debated and changed. - Civic education. We produce plain language guides to how the state government works. CRGD is non partisan. This vertical does not support or oppose any party, and its researchers follow CRGD's policy on political neutrality.

title: Urbanisation
summary: How a state where town and village blur into each other can plan for housing, water, waste, transport and public space.
body: Urban planning and land use Housing Water supply and sanitation Solid waste management Municipal finance and governance Public space How should planning work in places that are urban in character but rural in administration? What is the most effective way to manage solid waste in dense, mixed settlements? How can municipalities raise more of their own revenue fairly? What kind of housing do young families and migrant workers need, and who will build it? Much of Kerala is neither clearly urban nor clearly rural. Census figures over recent decades have shown a large rise in places with urban characteristics that are still governed as panchayats. This continuum creates particular challenges for planning and services. Why it matters Waste management failures, water shortages, flooding in towns and rising housing costs are urban problems that affect most of the state's population. Municipal governments have limited revenue and capacity. Planning laws were largely designed for a sharper distinction between town and country. How we work - Settlement studies. We map how places are changing and how they are governed. - Service delivery. We study water, sanitation and waste systems in specific towns and panchayats. - Municipal finance. We analyse property tax, user charges and grants. - Housing. We study housing demand, rental markets and public housing programs. The vertical works closely with Mobility, Environment and Federalism, and with elected representatives in urban local bodies.

title: Elections, Narratives and Perceptions
summary: How citizens form political opinions, how elections are fought, and how narratives, media and misinformation shape public perceptions of policy.
body: Electoral behaviour and turnout Campaigns and political communication Misinformation and fact checking Media and public opinion Survey methods Electoral reform What do voters in Kerala care about when they choose, and how is that changing? How do policy debates become political narratives, and what is lost along the way? How does misinformation spread in Malayalam, and what slows it down? How can opinion surveys be made more transparent and more reliable? Public policy is shaped by what people believe as much as by what is true. This vertical studies elections, political communication and public opinion, and the space between evidence and perception. Why it matters Kerala has high turnout and a highly engaged electorate. Political messages now travel through television, newspapers, social media and messaging groups, often in Malayalam, and often faster than they can be checked. Understanding how opinions form helps policymakers communicate honestly and helps citizens evaluate what they hear. How we work - Electoral analysis. We analyse published election results and turnout over time. - Narrative studies. We track how specific policy issues are framed in media and politics. - Information integrity. We study misinformation and the effectiveness of responses to it. - Survey research. We design and publish surveys with full methodology and data. All survey work follows CRGD's research standards, including publication of questionnaires, sampling methods, and margins of error.

title: Foreign Policy and Global Affairs
summary:
The Foreign Policy and Global Affairs vertical at CRGD examines the forces shaping India’s engagement with the world and the wider transformation of the international order. Its work covers foreign policy, diplomacy, geopolitics, international institutions, regional and global security, strategic partnerships, economic statecraft, multilateralism, and emerging transnational challenges.

The vertical seeks to produce rigorous, policy-relevant research that connects global developments with India’s strategic interests, democratic values, development priorities, and institutional choices. It also aims to create a platform for scholars, practitioners, and emerging researchers to engage with contemporary debates in international relations through research, commentary, dialogue, and public scholarship.

title: Peace, Conflict and Security
summary:
The Peace, Conflict and Security vertical at CRGD examines the causes, dynamics, and consequences of conflict, as well as the institutions and strategies that support peace, stability, and reconciliation. Its work spans conflict prevention, peacebuilding, mediation, security, humanitarian challenges, post-conflict reconstruction, identity and political violence, and the role of states, communities, and international institutions.

The vertical aims to produce policy-relevant research that connects theoretical insight with practical approaches to preventing violence, strengthening resilience, and building more peaceful, inclusive, and accountable societies.

title: Workshop: Writing Policy Briefs That Get Read
summary: A practical one day workshop for researchers, students and civil society professionals on turning research into short, persuasive briefs for decision makers.
body: mentor-one CRGD office, Pulimoodu Workshop Good research often fails to influence policy because it is not written for the people who make decisions. This workshop teaches the craft of the policy brief: choosing the question, putting the conclusion first, presenting evidence clearly and making recommendations that are specific and feasible. You will - analyse examples of effective and ineffective briefs - learn a simple structure that works for most briefs - draft a brief on a topic of your choice - receive feedback from the facilitator and other participants Participants should bring a laptop and a topic, ideally based on their own research or work. [Placeholder event.]

title: Webinar: Reading the Coast, Erosion, Ports and Communities
summary: An online discussion of how Kerala's coast is changing, and how decisions about sea walls, ports and relocation can be made more fairly.
body: scholar-two researcher-three Online Webinar Drawing on CRGD's long form essay The Sea Wall and the Shore, this webinar discusses coastal erosion, the effects of port development and the choices facing fishing communities. The speakers will present for twenty minutes, followed by questions from participants. The session will be recorded and published on this page. [Placeholder event.]

title: Kerala Policy Conclave 2026: Ageing, Work and Migration
summary: A two day conference on three forces reshaping Kerala's society and economy, with researchers, officials, employers, unions and civil society.
body: adviser-four fellow-one associate-one scholar-two [Conference venue] Conference Kerala's population is ageing quickly. The nature of work is changing. Patterns of migration out of, into and back to the state are shifting. Each of these is usually discussed on its own. The Kerala Policy Conclave brings them together, because their effects on families, public finances and the economy are closely connected. Day one: a society growing older - Opening address - Panel: Who will care for Kerala's older citizens? - Panel: Pensions, health costs and public finances - Presentation of CRGD's brief on a care guarantee Day two: work and migration - Panel: The Gulf comes home - Panel: Women, work and the missing growth engine - Panel: Workers from other states in Kerala's economy - Closing session: an agenda for the next five years Who should attend Policy makers, officials, researchers, employers, trade unions, civil society organisations, journalists and students. [Placeholder event. Confirm the venue, programme and speakers before publishing.]

title: Roundtable: Panchayat Finances After Three Decades
summary: Elected representatives, officials and researchers discuss the findings of CRGD's report on local government finances, and what reforms should come next.
body: scholar-one adviser-one CRGD office, Pulimoodu Roundtable This roundtable brings together presidents and members of panchayats and municipalities, officials of the local self government department, members of past State Finance Commissions and researchers to discuss the findings of CRGD's report Panchayat Finances After Three Decades of Decentralisation. Questions for discussion 1. How can local governments raise more of their own revenue fairly? 2. What would make the flow of funds from the state more predictable? 3. How can smaller panchayats get the technical support they need? 4. How can grama sabhas play a stronger role in reviewing spending? The discussion will follow the Chatham House Rule. A summary of the main points, without attribution, will be published afterwards. [Placeholder event.]

title: Founders' Lecture 2026: Why Public Policy Needs a Bridge
summary: The inaugural Founders' Lecture, on the distance between evidence, citizens and decision makers, and what an independent institution can do to close it.
body: [Venue name], near the Government Secretariat Lecture The Founders' Lecture is CRGD's annual public lecture on a question of lasting importance for public life in Kerala and India. In this inaugural lecture, CRGD's founder will reflect on why good evidence so often fails to reach the people who make decisions, why citizens are so rarely consulted before policy is made, and what an independent, non partisan institution can do about both. The lecture will be followed by questions from the audience. Programme - 5:00 pm Welcome - 5:10 pm Lecture - 5:55 pm Questions from the audience - 6:30 pm Close and tea Getting there The venue is a short walk from the Government Secretariat. Limited parking is available nearby; public transport is recommended. [Placeholder event. Confirm the venue, time and registration link before publishing.]

title: Colloquium: Return Migration, Work in Progress
summary: A research colloquium in which work in progress on return migration from the Gulf was presented to scholars and practitioners for critical feedback.
body: associate-one CRGD office, Pulimoodu Colloquium The colloquium discussed the early stages of CRGD's research on return migration, which later informed the long form essay The Gulf Comes Home. Participants raised questions about how to reach returnees who do not register with any agency, how to compare the experiences of men and women returnees, and how to separate the effects of the pandemic from longer term trends. [Placeholder event record.]

title: Report Launch and Panel: After the Landslides
summary: The launch of CRGD's special report on landslide risk in Kerala's hill districts, with a panel discussion on preparedness, land use and rehabilitation.
body: researcher-three scholar-three fellow-two [Venue name] Panel discussion CRGD launched its special report After the Landslides: Building Safer Hill Communities with a panel discussion. The authors presented the report's main recommendations: ward level susceptibility maps, community evacuation triggers tied to rainfall warnings, geological assessment before construction on steep slopes, and rehabilitation that gives families real choice. Panellists discussed the practical obstacles to each recommendation and the role of local governments and volunteers. [Placeholder event record.]

title: World Environment Day Dialogue: Living with a Changing Coast
summary: A dialogue held in a coastal community, bringing fishworkers, local representatives, engineers and researchers together to discuss erosion and protection.
body: scholar-two [Coastal community hall] Dialogue This dialogue was held in a coastal community rather than in a conference hall, so that the people most affected by coastal change could speak first. Fishworkers described the changes they had seen on their stretch of coast. Engineers explained the options for coastal protection and their limits. Local representatives spoke about the difficulty of planning when decisions are taken elsewhere. A note of the discussion, in Malayalam and English, was shared with participants and informed CRGD's later writing on the coast. [Placeholder event record.]

title: Budget Decoded 2026

title: About CRGD
summary: An independent, non-partisan research and advocacy institution dedicated to advancing liberty, knowledge, democracy, accountable governance, and development.
body: The Centre for Research on Governance and Development (CRGD): The Public Policy Bridge is an independent, non-partisan research and advocacy institution dedicated to advancing liberty, knowledge, democracy, accountable governance, and development. Founded on the conviction that public policy must be informed by evidence, guided by reason, and judged by its outcomes, CRGD seeks to bridge the divide between academic scholarship, institutions, and the realities of society. We undertake rigorous, inter/multi-disciplinary research, critically examine existing policies as well as practices, and develop innovative, practical solutions to complex civic, governance and development challenges. Rooted in profound intellectual vision and public purpose, we advance in-depth critical research, informed discourses and evidence-based policy action through scholarly publications, strategic partnerships and constructive engagement with policymakers and civil society, contributing to stronger institutions and meaningful institutional reforms. CRGD stands for the liberty, the responsibility to reason, and the imperative to reform and responsible interventions. Our Story From an Idea to an Institution The Centre for Research on Governance and Development (CRGD): The Public Policy Bridge was envisioned and founded by Amal Chandra , whose engagement with public affairs, policy research, and institutional processes revealed a persistent disconnect between academic knowledge, public decision-making and societal realities. Drawing on years of intellectual exchange, critical reflection, and collective brainstorming, he brought together diverse ideas, identified institutional gaps, and assembled a brilliant team committed to addressing them. A shared intellectual pursuit gradually evolved into a vision for an independent institution that connects scholarship with the practical demands of governance and development. The founding team comprises young professionals, all under thirty , with established records of academic achievement, research, publications, institutional leadership and international exposure. Their multidisciplinary experience spans public policy, scientific research, academia, civic engagement and collaborations with governments, research institutions and organisations across different levels. The vision acquired a structured institutional framework through The Statement Fellowship , a programme of Students For Liberty, during which Amal Chandra developed the proposal into an independent, non-profit research institution headquartered in Thiruvananthapuram, Keralam. CRGD is an entirely autonomous institution, neither affiliated with nor a constituent body of Students For Liberty. On 3 October 2026 , the founding General Body unanimously resolved to establish CRGD, adopting its constitutional framework and constituting its first Governing Body. Rooted in Keralam, nationally engaged and internationally oriented, CRGD embodies an ambition extending beyond the creation of another policy organisation: to build an enduring intellectual institution that questions established assumptions, connects knowledge with institutional practice, and contributes to consequential public policy and governance reforms. Its founding conviction remains that the enduring value of ideas lies in their capacity to inform decisions, strengthen institutions, and advance human progress. title: Accessibility
summary: Our commitment to making this website and our events usable by everyone, including people with disabilities.
body: CRGD wants everyone to be able to read our work and take part in our events. We aim for this website to meet the Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) 2.1 at level AA. What we have done - Text and background colours are chosen to meet contrast guidelines. - The website can be used with a keyboard alone, and focus is always visible. - A "skip to main content" link is the first item on every page. - Images have text descriptions, and decorative images are hidden from screen readers. - Pages use proper headings, lists and landmarks so assistive technology can navigate them. - Moving content, such as the latest updates strip, can be paused, and stops automatically if your device is set to reduce motion. - The website works at large text sizes and on small screens. - Publications are available as web pages as well as PDF files. Events Our venue arrangements aim to be accessible. When you register for an event, tell us about any requirements, such as step free access, sign language interpretation or materials in large print, and we will do our best to meet them. Known limitations Some older PDF documents and some embedded content from other services may not be fully accessible. If you need any content in a different format, please ask. Feedback If you find any part of this website difficult to use, please write to {{email}}. Tell us the page, the problem and the assistive technology you use, if any. We will reply within five working days.

title: Code of Conduct
summary: The standards of behaviour we expect from everyone who takes part in CRGD's work, events, programs and campus clubs.
body: CRGD brings together people of different ages, backgrounds, beliefs and political views. That is our strength, and it depends on everyone treating each other with respect. This code applies to staff, fellows, interns, coordinators, campus club members, speakers, participants in our events and anyone representing CRGD. We expect everyone to - treat others with courtesy and respect, especially when disagreeing - argue with ideas, not attack people - listen, and give others a fair chance to speak - respect the confidentiality of discussions held under the Chatham House Rule or other agreed terms - be honest about the evidence and about their own interests - look out for each other, and report concerns We do not accept - harassment of any kind, including sexual harassment - discrimination on the grounds of caste, religion, gender, sexual orientation, disability, age, region, language or political belief - intimidation, threats or abuse, in person or online - using a CRGD role or platform for party political campaigning - plagiarism or fabrication of evidence Prevention of sexual harassment CRGD is committed to a workplace free from sexual harassment, in line with the Sexual Harassment of Women at Workplace (Prevention, Prohibition and Redressal) Act, 2013. [Placeholder: give the details of the Internal Committee and how to contact it.] Raising a concern If you experience or witness behaviour that breaks this code, please tell the person in charge of the event or program, or write to {{email}}. Concerns are handled confidentially and promptly. No one will be penalised for raising a concern in good faith. Consequences Depending on the seriousness of the behaviour, CRGD may issue a warning, ask a person to leave an event, end their participation in a program, or end their association with CRGD.

title: Editorial Policy
summary: The principles and standards that govern everything CRGD publishes, from policy briefs and reports to commentary, podcasts and videos.
body: 1. Editorial Principles The Centre for Research on Governance and Development (CRGD) is committed to advancing independent scholarship, informed public discourse and intellectually credible policy analysis. Our editorial philosophy rests on the principles of intellectual independence, factual accuracy, methodological integrity, transparency, fairness and public relevance . We regard publishing as an exercise in intellectual responsibility. Every publication should contribute to knowledge, examine an important public question, challenge established assumptions where warranted, or offer substantive insights into governance, public policy and development. CRGD welcomes diverse perspectives, including arguments that question prevailing institutional practices or established policy positions. We do not require ideological conformity or agreement with the institution's published positions. All contributions, however, must meet our standards of evidence, reasoning, professional ethics and responsible expression. 2. Editorial Independence CRGD maintains editorial independence in the selection, assessment, development and publication of its content. Editorial decisions shall be guided by scholarly merit, originality, analytical quality, public significance and consistency with the institution's objectives. Political affiliation, institutional influence, financial contributions or personal relationships shall not determine editorial outcomes. Authors retain responsibility for their arguments and conclusions. Views expressed in individually authored publications are those of their respective authors and do not necessarily represent the institutional position of CRGD. Institutional publications, including official policy reports and statements, shall undergo the appropriate internal approval process. No donor, sponsor, partner or external stakeholder shall exercise editorial control over research findings or publication decisions. 3. Publications and Editorial Categories CRGD publishes research, analysis, commentary and more across the following categories, each serving a distinct intellectual and public purpose. 1. Policy Briefs: Concise, evidence-based assessments of specific policy problems, accompanied by actionable recommendations. 2. Long Form: Extended essays exploring complex political, economic, social and institutional questions in depth. 3. Policy Reports: Comprehensive research publications examining policy frameworks, institutional performance and reform alternatives. 4. Analysis: Structured, evidence-led examinations of contemporary developments, policy decisions, emerging trends and their wider implications. 5. Special Reports: Focused investigations and thematic studies addressing issues of exceptional public or institutional significance. 6. Commentary: Interpretative perspectives on contemporary affairs, public institutions and policy debates. 7. Explainers: Accessible, factually grounded examinations of complex concepts, issues, legislation, institutions and policy developments. 8. Opinion: Clearly articulated arguments presenting original perspectives on matters of public interest. 9. Blogs: Concise reflections, observations and discussions exploring emerging issues, experiences and ideas. 10. Young Thoughts: A dedicated platform for students and emerging thinkers to contribute original ideas, critical reflections and informed perspectives. 11. Expert View: Specialist contributions from scholars, practitioners and professionals drawing upon recognised expertise and experience. 12. Reviews: Critical assessments of publications, policies, intellectual contributions and other works of public or academic significance. 13. Books and Journals: Scholarly discussions, reviews and assessments of books, academic journals and significant research literature. 14. Internship/Fellowship Reports: Selected research outputs, field observations and analytical reports developed through CRGD's internship/fellowship programmes. 15. Podcas

title: Frequently Asked Questions
summary: Short answers to the questions people most often ask about CRGD.
body: About CRGD What is CRGD? The Centre for Research on Governance and Development (CRGD): The Public Policy Bridge is an independent, non-partisan research and advocacy institution dedicated to advancing liberty, knowledge, democracy, accountable governance, and development. It is headquartered in Thiruvananthapuram, Keralam. Read about CRGD. Is CRGD part of the government? No. CRGD is independent of government. It may carry out research commissioned by public bodies, but only on terms that protect its independence. See independence and funding. Is CRGD linked to a political party? No. CRGD is non partisan. It does not accept funding from political parties and does not support or oppose any party or candidate. Who funds CRGD? Individual supporters, foundations, research grants and, under strict conditions, commissioned work. Major sources are listed in our annual reports. Research and publications Can I read CRGD's publications for free? Yes. All our publications are free to read online and to download. Can I republish a CRGD article? Most of our publications can be republished free of charge with credit. See copyright and republishing. How do I suggest a research topic? Write to us through the contact page. We read every suggestion, and several of our projects began this way. Can I write for CRGD? Yes. See submissions for what we publish and how to pitch. I found an error in a publication. What should I do? Please tell us through the contact page. We correct errors promptly and openly, as described in our editorial policy. Programs and learning Who can apply for fellowships and internships? Eligibility differs by program. Each program page lists who can apply, the duration, the stipend and how to apply. Do I need to be from Kerala? No. Many programs welcome applicants from across India. Some field work requires the ability to speak Malayalam, which will be stated in the call. How do I start a CRGD Policy Club at my college? See campus clubs. You will need a faculty supporter and a small group of interested students. Are CRGD Academy courses free? Some are free; others charge a modest fee to cover costs, with scholarships for those who need them. Fees are stated on each course page. Events Are CRGD events open to the public? Most are, and most are free. Some roundtables are invitation only so that participants can speak freely; we usually publish a summary afterwards. Are events recorded? Public lectures and panels are usually recorded and published on the event page and our video channel. Media How can journalists reach CRGD's researchers? See media enquiries.

title: Founder's Message
summary: A message from Amal Chandra, Founder and President of the Centre for Research on Governance and Development (CRGD).
body: Ideas acquire public value when they challenge assumptions, inform decisions, and improve institutions with global visibility. To me, public policy is applied political science. The defining challenges of our time are not just economic or political; they are fundamentally questions of civil society and governance. How societies create and distribute opportunity, protect liberty, exercise public power, and respond to emerging challenges depends on the quality of their laws, institutions, and the evidence informing their decisions. India's remarkable economic and democratic journey illustrates both the possibilities of progress and the persistence of institutional contradictions. Economic growth has not eliminated inequality of opportunity; technological advancement has not automatically ensured accountability; and democratic participation, however extensive, cannot substitute for institutional integrity, constitutional safeguards and informed public deliberation. The Centre for Research on Governance and Development (CRGD): The Public Policy Bridge was founded to engage seriously with these questions and beyond, thus contributing to more rigorous, independent and solutions-oriented public policy interventions. Our conviction is fundamental: research must challenge conventions and advance understanding; advocacy must be grounded in reason rather than rhetoric; and public policy must transcend political expediency to confront structural challenges. Their ultimate worth lies not in the ideas they generate or the attention they command, but in the institutions they improve, the reforms they enable, and the enduring public value they create. CRGD is committed to intellectual independence, methodological rigour and constructive engagement across ideological and institutional boundaries. Our non-partisanship does not imply indifference to democratic principles, institutional failures or the misuse of public authority. Rather, it demands that we assess policies consistently, question power responsibly and allow evidence, not political allegiance, to shape our conclusions. We seek to bring together global scholars, policymakers, practitioners and emerging thinkers to generate original research, encourage critical dialogue and develop practical responses to pressing policy challenges. Our commitment to liberty, reason, constitutional democracy, economic opportunity and accountable governance will remain central to this endeavour. We recognise that no single institution or intellectual tradition holds a monopoly over good ideas. Progress depends on openness to disagreement, the willingness to revise established assumptions and the capacity to translate knowledge into responsible action in liberty. Our ambition is not simply to add another institution to the policy landscape, but to establish one whose credibility rests on the quality of its research, whose independence is evident in the integrity of its work, and whose relevance is demonstrated through its contributions. At CRGD, we believe that ideas must withstand scrutiny, institutions must be responsible, and development must ultimately enlarge human freedom. Amal Chandra \ Founder and President\ Centre for Research on Governance and Development (CRGD) Read more about our founder.

title: Independence and Funding
summary: How CRGD is funded, what it will and will not accept, and how it protects the independence of its research.
body: A think tank is only as useful as it is trustworthy. Readers need to know that our conclusions are our own, and not those of whoever paid for the work. This page explains the rules we follow. Our principles 1. Conclusions are not for sale. No funder, partner or government body may determine, edit or veto our findings or recommendations. 2. We publish what we find. We do not accept funding that allows a funder to suppress results it dislikes. 3. We are non partisan. We do not accept money from political parties, and we do not campaign for or against any party or candidate. 4. We are transparent. We disclose our sources of funding, and we disclose the funder of each specific project in the publication itself. Sources of funding CRGD may be supported by: - donations from individuals who share our aims - grants from philanthropic foundations and trusts - research grants from Indian and international academic or public bodies - commissioned research from government bodies, under the conditions below - fees for courses and programs run by the CRGD Academy, set to recover costs and supported by scholarships Conditions for commissioned work When a government department, public body or private organisation commissions research from us, the agreement must state that: - CRGD retains full control over methods, analysis and conclusions - CRGD may publish the findings, after any agreed and limited period for review of factual accuracy - the commissioning body is named in the publication We decline commissions that do not meet these conditions. What we do not accept - funding from political parties or their affiliated organisations - funding conditional on reaching a particular conclusion - anonymous donations above a threshold set by the Governing Board - funding from sources that the Governing Board judges would damage public trust in our work Disclosure Our annual reports list our major sources of funding. Each publication carries a note naming any specific funder of that work. Conflicts of interest Researchers, board members and advisers declare relevant interests, including employment, consultancy, shareholdings and close family relationships. Where an interest could reasonably be seen to affect a piece of work, it is disclosed or the person steps away from that work. Questions If you have questions about our funding or believe our independence has been compromised in any way, please write to us. Concerns about independence are reported to the Governing Board.

title: How We Work
summary: We approach public policy as a discipline of inquiry, judgment, and institutional responsibility.
body: At CRGD, we approach public policy as a discipline of inquiry, judgment, and institutional responsibility. Our work begins by asking the questions that matter: what is failing, why existing approaches fall short, whose interests are affected, and what alternatives can produce better outcomes. We examine issues in their political, economic, social and institutional contexts, recognising that sound policy requires more than technical expertise; it demands historical understanding, intellectual openness and an appreciation of practical realities. Our approach rests on four interconnected principles: 1. Investigate with Independence 2. Think Across Disciplines 3. Engage Across Institutions 4. Translate Ideas into Action We value intellectual integrity, substantive engagement, and long-term institutional outcomes. Our research and recommendations remain open to scrutiny, revision, and new evidence.

title: Our Founder
summary: Amal Chandra, Founder, President, and CEO of the Centre for Research on Governance and Development (CRGD): The Public Policy Bridge
body: About the Founder Amal Chandra is an author, public policy analyst, political commentator, and columnist whose work focuses on democracy, governance, strategic affairs, accountability, and public policy. He serves as National Affairs Editor at The Open Tab and as The Statement Fellow and South Asia Coordinator at Students For Liberty (SFL). His debut book, The Essential (2023), features a foreword by Adv. Salman Khurshid, former Union Minister of External Affairs, and was launched by Dr. Shashi Tharoor alongside Adv. V.D. Satheesan, the current CM of Keralam. His professional experience spans government, public policy research, development programmes and parliamentary affairs. He previously worked with the Kerala Development and Innovation Strategic Council (K-DISC), the PMPY–UNICEF programme at the Central University of Gujarat, and the Centre for Public Policy Research (CPPR) through a youth leadership fellowship in collaboration with Atlas Network, USA. He has worked closely with Dr. Shashi Tharoor and served as a Policy Officer of the Congress party and a Research Associate to Adv. Dean Kuriakose, Member of Parliament. He has also held student leadership positions at University College, Thiruvananthapuram, and Pondicherry Central University. A Gold Medallist in Political Science and a participant in international liberty and public policy forums, Chandra contributes extensively to national and international policy discourse. His writings and research contributions have appeared in publications and platforms including the American Institute for Economic Research, Observer Research Foundation, Indian Journal of Public Administration , Global Policy , Modern Diplomacy , South Asia Voices , East Asia Forum , SAGE, and The UnPopulist . Read the Founder's Message or view Amal Chandra's profile.

title: Research Standards
summary: The review process, ethical rules and data practices that every CRGD publication must meet.
body: Review before publication Publication type Minimum review --- --- Policy reports, special reports, books Internal review by a senior researcher, and external review by at least one independent expert Policy briefs, analysis, long form Internal review by a senior researcher not involved in the work Commentary, explainers, blogs Editorial review for accuracy, fairness and clarity Opinion, expert view, young thoughts Editorial review for accuracy and adherence to the editorial policy; views remain the author's Reviewers check whether the evidence supports the conclusions, whether alternative explanations have been considered, whether the methods are described clearly enough to be repeated, and whether the writing is fair to people and positions discussed. Research ethics Research involving people follows these rules: - Informed consent. Participants are told what the research is for, how their information will be used, and that they can decline or withdraw at any time. - Privacy. Personal information is kept secure and is never published in a form that identifies an individual without their consent. - Care for vulnerable participants. Additional safeguards apply to research with children, persons in custody, survivors of violence and others at risk. - No harm. We do not pursue research that could foreseeably put participants in danger. Projects that involve sensitive subjects or vulnerable participants are reviewed by an ethics panel before field work begins. Data and transparency - We describe our data sources and methods in every publication. - Where licences and privacy allow, we publish the data behind our charts and tables. - We say clearly when findings are preliminary or uncertain. - Surveys are published with questionnaires, sample design and margins of error. Use of artificial intelligence tools Researchers may use software tools, including AI tools, to assist with tasks such as transcription, translation drafts, data cleaning and coding. They may not use such tools to generate findings, quotations or references, and all output is checked by a person. The researcher remains responsible for every word published. Corrections Errors are corrected promptly and transparently. See our editorial policy.

title: Submissions
summary: How to submit commentary, opinion, expert views, reviews and student writing for publication by CRGD.
body: CRGD welcomes contributions from researchers, practitioners, students and citizens who have something useful to say about public policy. We are particularly keen to hear from people with direct experience of the issues they write about. What we accept Series Who it is for Length --- --- --- Expert View Practitioners and scholars with long experience in a field 1,200 to 2,000 words Opinion Anyone with a well argued view on a policy question 800 to 1,200 words Commentary Timely responses to policy developments 600 to 1,000 words Reviews Reviews of books, reports and policy documents 800 to 1,500 words Young Thoughts Students and people under 25, including campus club members 600 to 1,200 words Blogs Field notes, reflections and short analysis 500 to 1,000 words We do not normally publish unsolicited full length research reports, but we are happy to discuss collaboration on research ideas. How to submit 1. Send a pitch first. Email a short pitch of no more than 200 words to the submissions address below. Tell us the argument, why it matters now, and why you are the right person to write it. 2. We reply within ten working days. If we are interested, an editor will agree length, deadline and focus with you. 3. Write and submit the draft as an editable document, with sources linked or listed at the end. 4. Editing. An editor will work with you on structure, clarity and accuracy. You will approve the final version before publication. Send pitches to {{submissionsEmail}} with "Pitch:" and your proposed title in the subject line. Our expectations - The piece must be your original work and not published elsewhere, unless agreed in advance. - Factual claims must be supported by sources we can check. - Disclose any interest that a reader would consider relevant, such as employment, funding or political affiliation. - Write in plain language. Avoid jargon and acronyms where you can. - Respect people you disagree with. We do not publish personal attacks. Young Thoughts The Young Thoughts series is mentored. Student writers are paired with a CRGD researcher who helps them develop their argument and their evidence. It is a good place for a first publication. Campus club members can also submit through their club coordinator. title: Work with Us
summary: What it is like to work at CRGD, who we look for, and how our hiring process works.
body: CRGD is a small institution with large ambitions. Everyone here does real work from the first week: researchers write, program staff teach, and everyone talks to the people our work is meant to serve. Who we look for We hire for curiosity, care and clarity. - Curiosity. You want to understand how things actually work, not just how they are supposed to work. - Care with evidence. You check sources, question your own assumptions and say clearly what you do not know. - Clarity. You can explain a complicated idea to a busy person in a few sentences. - Public spirit. You want your work to be useful to people beyond your own field. Formal qualifications matter less than these qualities. We welcome applicants from all disciplines and backgrounds, including people who have worked in government, journalism, civil society, law, business or the armed forces. What we offer - Meaningful work on questions that affect millions of people - Mentoring from experienced researchers and practitioners - Time for learning, including support for courses and conferences - A collegial, non hierarchical workplace where junior colleagues are heard - Fair pay, published in each job advertisement How we hire 1. Application. A CV, a short cover letter and, for research roles, one writing sample. 2. Shortlisting. Every application is read by at least two people. We aim to tell every applicant the outcome. 3. Task. Shortlisted candidates complete a short, paid task similar to the work of the role. 4. Conversation. An interview with the people you would work with most closely. 5. Decision. We aim to decide within three weeks of the closing date. Equal opportunity CRGD is an equal opportunity employer. We actively encourage applications from women, persons with disabilities, people from Scheduled Castes, Scheduled Tribes and other historically marginalised communities, and people from outside the major cities. Tell us about any adjustments you need during the hiring process and we will make them. Current openings See current openings, or explore fellowships and internships if you are earlier in your career. summary: Short, structured courses on specific skills and subjects: public finance, policy writing, data for governance, and more. Most run online on weekday evenings, so working people can take them.

title: Dialogue
summary: Dialogues bring people who disagree into the same room under rules that let them speak plainly. They are small, prepared in advance and followed by a written note of what was learned.

title: Academic Programs
summary: Programs designed with universities and colleges: credit bearing electives, faculty development, dissertation supervision and field placements in policy research.

title: Collaborations
summary: Joint research, teaching and events with universities, research institutions, civil society organisations and public bodies, in India and abroad.

title: Colloquium
summary: A regular forum where researchers present work in progress to a critical audience before it is published. Open to scholars and students; papers are circulated a week in advance.

title: Advocacy
summary: Sustained, evidence based efforts to change a specific policy or practice, carried out openly and on the record.

title: Ongoing
summary: Projects and engagements that are under way, with their objectives, partners and current status.

title: Accomplished
summary: Completed projects and the results they produced, stated as precisely as the evidence allows.

title: Awards and Honours
summary: Recognition received by CRGD and its people for their work.

title: Press Releases
summary: Official statements and announcements from CRGD.

title: Photographs
summary: Photographs from CRGD events, field work and programs. Images may be used by the press with credit to CRGD.

title: Interviews
summary: Interviews given by CRGD's people to newspapers, television, radio and digital media.

title: Speeches
summary: Texts and recordings of speeches and lectures delivered by CRGD's leadership and researchers.

title: Archives
summary: Older material from CRGD's history: early statements, event records and documents preserved for reference.

title: CRGD in News
summary: News coverage of CRGD's research, events and people.

title: Mentions
summary: Places where CRGD's work has been cited or referred to: in the press, in legislatures, in official documents and in academic writing.
